The NASA goals call for 33% reductions in block fuel burn and takeoff field length, 60% reduction in NO emissions below CAEP/6 standards, and certification noise levels 32 cumulative EPNdB under current Stage 4/Chapter 4 noise limits.

The independent design variables include sea level static thrust, wing reference area, aerodynamic design point fan pressure ratio, overall pressure ratio, fan drive system architecture, bypass nozzle architecture, and the high- and low-pressure compressor work split.
The objective functions include ramp weight, fuel burn, noise (cumulative margin relative to Stage 4/Chapter 4 noise limits), and oxides of nitrogen (NO ) emissions.

The thermodynamic engine cycle performance is analyzed using the Numerical Propulsion System Simulation (NPSS) code, and the aeromechanical design, flowpath, and engine weight analyses are performed with the Weight Analysis of Turbine Engines (WATE) code.

The aircraft synthesis and sizing analyses are carried out using NASA's Flight Optimization System (FLOPS) computer program, with enhancements to the FLOPS capabilities to better model the impacts of large, ultra-high bypass ratio engines.

Detailed takeoff and approach trajectory calculations are automatically made for every airplane and engine design, capturing the influence of airplane trajectory and engine throttling on noise certification.
The NO emissions are estimated based on the high-temperature regions inside the engine combustor, where nitrogen in the air oxidizes into nitric oxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO ).

The optimized solutions provide insight into the ultra-high bypass engine design process and help guide NASA's technology development efforts to achieve the aggressive performance, noise, and emissions goals for the new single-aisle aircraft.

Significant fuel and cost reductions, as well as substantial reductions in noise and emissions, are necessary to justify the development of a new single-aisle transport or to retrofit current aircraft with new engines, enabling unconstrained aviation growth without negatively impacting the environment.

The key challenges in the design of ultra-high bypass turbofan engines include managing the shaft speed mismatch between the low-pressure turbine and the low-pressure fan, as well as the high hot section temperatures in the engine due to the high bypass ratio.

The notional airplane is based on an analytical evolution of the currently-in-service Boeing 737-800 with winglets, with a design cruise Mach number increased from 0.785 to 0.800 and a range increase from 3060 to 3250 nm.

The 162-passenger, mixed-class, single-aisle cabin arrangement is maintained, and broad use of composite structural materials is assumed, resulting in a 15% reduction in the component weights computed for the wing, fuselage, and empennage.

The low-speed trajectory analysis is validated for the baseline airframe model using performance data of a 737 taking off and landing under standard day, dry runway conditions, with the same analysis used to predict the trajectories of the advanced airframe model.
A noise abatement throttle cutback occurs in all cases between 16,000 and 17,000 ft from brake release, with the engine climb thrust reduced to the minimum level permitted by regulation.

Because of its lower specific thrust relative to the CFM56-7B, a throttle cutback for a UHB engine designed to meet a rolling takeoff thrust target is typically not as deep (in percent thrust), and a typical UHB-powered airplane does not climb as high over the flyover measurement point as the 737 reference model does.
